La gentrification des quartiers populair: The gentrification of working-class neighbourhoods is pushing marginalized families into precarity. Photo: Ridolphe Aristil
« J’ai une audience le 20 juillet, et j’: “I have a hearing on July 20, and I’m waiting to see what happens,” Mr. Boujemaa, who prefers not to give his first name, told us last month, his voice anxious. The father is one of many Montréal tenants who have to leave their homes, and are therefore threatened with eviction, because of their landlord’s renovations.
Une bataille de longue haleine dans La P: A long-haul battle in La Petite-Patrie
Depuis 2015, le propriétaire de l’immeub: Since 2015, the owner of the building where Mr. Boujemaa lives has been trying everything to evict him from his apartment in La Petite-Patrie. “In 2015, he told me he would do everything he could to make me leave my apartment,” he says. “He told me: ‘This is Canada, you’ll see.’” That was the threat the man made, knowing his tenant is an immigrant.
Depuis, chaque année, M. Boujemaa se ren: Since then, every year, Mr. Boujemaa has gone to the Tribunal administratif du logement (TAL) to defend his right to stay in his home. His greatest fear is that his family will be uprooted. “Last year, the landlord told me he had sold my apartment to his brother-in-law. He told me it was an eviction so his daughter could take over the unit,” says the father of two. The judge ruled in the tenant’s favour after finding an error in the file. “The story about the landlord’s niece wanting my apartment wasn’t true,” he says.
Deux mois après ces événements, une entr: Two months after these events, a construction company contacted Mr. Boujemaa. According to him, the landlord wanted to convert the duplex that houses the family’s apartment into a single-family home. The contractor had managed to obtain a permit, even though no architect had ever come into Mr. Boujemaa’s home to take measurements for the work. “Today, I’m the only one living in this duplex. They evicted the tenants in the other units last summer. The building’s lot is for sale. They’re just waiting for me to leave to start their project,” he says apprehensively.
Le quartier de Parc-Extension est partic: The Parc-Extension neighbourhood is particularly affected by renovictions. Photo: Ridolphe Aristil

The Parc-Extension neighbourhood is particularly affected by renovictions. Many people there are going through situations similar to Mr. Boujemaa’s. Yet when you walk through the neighbourhood’s lively streets, this reality is invisible.
Des marchands sont sur le pas de la port: Shopkeepers stand in the doorways of their businesses, asking customers how they’re doing. In front of their stalls overflowing with colourful fruits and vegetables, a swarm of strollers and children fills the sidewalks, accompanied by their parents or early childhood educators. Under the awnings of restaurants, old friends chat and laugh, sitting on plastic chairs, cigarettes in hand. It’s hard to believe that a much darker reality hides in these streets brimming with joie de vivre. Cases of renovictions punctuate the daily life of Rizwan Khan, a community worker with the Comité d’Action de Parc-Extension (CAPE).
Chaque jour, le CAPE gère des crises de: Every day, CAPE manages housing crises. Mr. Khan takes us to 7434 Querbes Street, an unremarkable four-storey red brick building. Empty for over a year, the quadruplex has been the scene of evictions. The community worker says the owner offered his tenants sums of money to get them to leave. “Most of the tenants at 7434 Querbes ended up moving and finding housing elsewhere. Two stayed until the end. There were people without status, newcomers, families, very elderly and vulnerable people,” says Mr. Khan. One woman had lived there for decades. “Technically, under the law, she couldn’t even be evicted. The Civil Code protects low-income people over 75 who have lived somewhere for more than 10 years. But she was put out, like everyone else,” the community worker laments. The owner managed to get around the law by forcing her to agree to leave herself.
Le 7434, rue Querbes a été revendu, et l: 7434 Querbes was resold, and the owner made a profit of several hundred thousand dollars. The new owner removed all of the fire safety systems, which is illegal. After that move, firefighters had to step in and evacuate the building for safety reasons. Without the fire safety systems, it was impossible for tenants to move back into their homes. According to Mr. Khan, this is a way for the new owner to carry out illegal evictions. “The justification is that he’s rebuilding the building and has to remove everything inside,” he says. In a few months, these apartments will be refurbished and ready for new rentals. “Wealthier people will live there, because rents will have doubled or tripled,” the community worker predicts.
Depuis que le nouveau campus de l’Univer: Since the Université de Montréal’s new campus opened in the neighbourhood in 2018, renovictions have accelerated. Knowing that university students and professionals who work at the university can afford to pay higher rents, landlords are redoubling their efforts to drive out their former tenants and renovate the units. These tenants are forced to move farther and farther from the city centre or to pay double their old rent for a unit that is often of poor quality.
Non loin de là, nous nous arrêtons devan: Not far from there, we stop in front of a building that suffered a similar fate. 555-561 Saint-Roch Street is a two-storey red brick duplex next to a grocery store. The building, with its dilapidated doors, contrasts with the walls of the church at the same intersection, decorated with biblical scenes. The babbling and joyful racket of children playing reach us through the half-open balcony door of a second-floor apartment.
C’était la trame sonore des appartements: That was the soundtrack of the neighbouring apartments when they were occupied. “A Pakistani family lived there,” says Mr. Khan, pointing to the next-door unit. “Two brothers, their wives, their children, the grandmother,” he adds about his former clients, some of whom were newcomers while the others had been here longer. The building’s owner tried to evict them by telling them he was going to house a member of his own family in their apartment. He offered them $10,000 to leave. The family consulted CAPE, and a file was opened at the TAL. During the proceedings, language barriers complicated matters, as the family spoke only English and their mother tongue. They ended up leaving their home.
Les défis linguistiques ne sont pas chos: Language challenges are not uncommon. Guiying Wang, a community worker at the Service à la famille chinoise, regularly receives calls from allophone residents facing eviction threats. She helps these people, who speak neither French nor English, find their way through the great labyrinth of Quebec housing rights.
Les besoins sont tels que Mme Wang est c: The needs are such that Ms. Wang is constantly overwhelmed by calls, which come in on several phone lines at once. “If they don’t speak French or English, we tell them to write a summary of their situation in Chinese. Then we help them translate it and communicate their situation to the tenants’ committee in their borough,” Ms. Wang explains. Unfortunately, the organization doesn’t have the resources to provide support throughout the proceedings. “We strongly encourage them to ask for help from family or friends who are more comfortable in French and English,” she explains. If they have to appear at the TAL, the organization provides its clients with translators, lawyers and social workers who speak different Chinese dialects. Despite this, acts of intimidation by landlords abound, as they particularly target tenants who don’t know their rights or the language. Tenants in Parc-Extension are targeted for renovations for similar reasons. “On paper, the recourse exists. Someone can go to court, contest, show that their landlord is acting in bad faith or didn’t properly plan their project, and win,” says Mr. Khan.
Mais entrer en contact avec les plaignan: But getting in touch with complainants is difficult because of the language barrier. “It’s also hard to let tenants know their rights, because everything is in French. They aren’t aware that CAPE exists, so they resign themselves to their fate,” he says sadly. The fact that many tenants already live in precarity, on top of having other responsibilities and being swamped with work and family, only makes their situation worse. Often, they have no time, money or energy left to fight to stay in their homes. And the challenges don’t end there. Even if tenants manage to overcome these obstacles and submit their case to the tribunal, barriers remain. “There’s also a shortage of lawyers to represent tenants. So even if there is access to justice—which isn’t always the case—there’s a lack of lawyers, even at CAPE.” It is this shortage of housing lawyers that led Mr. Khan to study law. “Even if these populations know their rights, do they have the means to protect themselves?”
Selon Leslie Touré Kapo, chercheur en sé: According to Leslie Touré Kapo, an urban security researcher, these many obstacles are part of the systemic barriers that affect residents of working-class neighbourhoods more broadly. “The question is whether these populations dealing with precarious situations know their rights. And even if they know their rights, do they have the means to protect themselves?” he asks. “We have to take into account the mental load of legal proceedings. Someone who works two jobs in the same day doesn’t necessarily have the time and energy. We need to ask ourselves about the workload that people in working-class neighbourhoods who take legal action actually bear,” he explains. The researcher believes the city must examine the accessibility of legal recourse for Montréal’s most marginalized and most precarious tenants.
Ce genre de barrière systémique a eu rai: This kind of systemic barrier got the better of Mr. Boujemaa. Almost two weeks after our first conversation, he informs us that his hearing has been postponed to mid-August and that it’s hopeless. “I have to leave, I don’t stand a chance. The lawyer told me my landlord had the building permit, that all his documents were in order. He found the loophole,” he tells us, panicking. “I’m looking for another apartment and I haven’t found anything. The apartments I’ve visited are unsanitary and full of mould, with rents of $1,200 or $1,300. It’s hell!” he says in despair. He especially doesn’t want to move far from La Petite-Patrie, because otherwise his children would have to travel more than an hour to keep attending their high school. “I’ve visited three apartments very close by. I didn’t get an answer after I filled out the application for one of them. Another was extremely unsanitary. It’s a disaster,” he exclaims. Being forced to move in the middle of a pandemic only adds to the stress of Mr. Boujemaa, who is desperately looking for help. “I have to be out before August 31, otherwise I’ll be on the street. I’m looking, my wife is looking, we’re visiting places. I don’t see the light at the end of the tunnel.”
